sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a stateless, request-response application-layer protocol that runs over TCP (or QUIC for HTTP/3) and defines how clients and servers exchange resources using methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH), status codes (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx), and headers.
HTTP is the lingua franca of the web. Every browser tab, every mobile API call, every microservice-to-microservice RPC over REST, and an increasing share of IoT traffic is HTTP. The protocol is text-oriented (in HTTP/1.x) and conceptually simple: a client sends a request line (`GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1`), a set of headers (`Host:`, `Accept:`, `Authorization:`), an empty line, and an optional body; the server replies with a status line (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK`), its own headers, an empty line, and the response body. HTTP is stateless, meaning each request carries all the context the server needs (including cookies for session continuity) — the protocol itself remembers nothing, which is what makes it horizontally scalable: any server can handle any request, because there is no per-connection server state required by the spec. The methods encode intent: GET is safe and idempotent (no side effects, repeatable), PUT and DELETE are idempotent (same effect if repeated), POST is neither (each call may create a new resource), and PATCH is for partial updates. Status codes partition outcomes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

Why does HTTP matter in real systems? Because almost every public API in the world is HTTP, and the protocol's evolution from HTTP/1.0 to HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 to HTTP/3 directly shapes performance. HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection per request, paying the handshake cost every time. HTTP/1.1 introduced keep-alive (default `Connection: keep-alive`) so a TCP connection could carry multiple sequential requests, plus pipelining (rarely used because of head-of-line blocking). HTTP/2 (2015, based on Google's SPDY) introduced multiplexing — many parallel streams over a single TCP connection — plus header compression (HPACK) and binary framing. HTTP/3 (2022) replaces TCP with QUIC to eliminate head-of-line blocking at the transport layer and to combine transport + TLS handshakes into 1 RTT. Real-world: GitHub migrated to HTTP/2 in 2016 and reported significant reductions in page-load time, especially for users with high RTT; Cloudflare deployed HTTP/3 broadly in 2020 and saw mobile latency improvements of 10–30%. Netflix streams video over HTTP using chunked transfer encoding (HTTP/1.1) and range requests, which lets the player adaptively switch bitrates mid-stream — ABR (Adaptive Bitrate Streaming) over HTTP is the foundation of almost all modern video delivery.

Real-world: Amazon's product page makes 50–100 HTTP calls per page load (recommendations, reviews, inventory, pricing), and the design choice to use REST over HTTP for inter-service communication is what allows Amazon's hundreds of independent service teams to evolve independently. Instagram's feed service makes parallel HTTP calls to media, likes, and comments backends, using HTTP/2 multiplexing to fit them all in one TCP connection. The trade-off: HTTP's text format and per-request header overhead make it inefficient for high-throughput, small-message workloads — which is why Kafka uses a binary protocol, gRPC uses Protobuf over HTTP/2, and GraphQL exists to reduce the number of HTTP round-trips needed to assemble a complex view. A common pitfall is treating HTTP as "just a transport" and ignoring its semantics: if your POST is non-idempotent but your client retries on 5xx, you will create duplicate orders. The fix is to design for idempotency using idempotency keys (Stripe's pattern) or to make the operation naturally idempotent (use PUT with a client-generated ID).

HTTP's statelessness is also its superpower for reliability. Because any server can handle any request, HTTP services scale horizontally by adding instances behind a load balancer, with no need for session affinity (sticky sessions). When sticky sessions are needed (e.g., WebSocket or a legacy app that caches per-instance), they introduce a load-balancing pathology: a hot instance gets overloaded while others idle. Modern designs avoid this by externalizing session state to Redis or a shared cache. The other key concept is content negotiation: the `Accept` header lets the client say "give me JSON or Protobuf or JPEG," and the `Content-Type` header on the response tells the client what it got. This is how a single API endpoint can serve HTML to browsers, JSON to mobile apps, and Protobuf to internal microservices. Finally, idempotency is the cornerstone of robust distributed systems: a payment API must be designed so that a retried POST after a network timeout is safe, typically by including an `Idempotency-Key` header that the server uses to deduplicate.

HTTP connects to nearly every other concept: HTTPS (Topic 4) wraps it in TLS, load balancers (Phase 5) operate at L7 on HTTP semantics, REST APIs are HTTP, and GraphQL is HTTP with a single POST endpoint. Latency budgets (Phase 1, Topic 8) must account for HTTP overhead: a typical REST call has 200–800 bytes of headers, plus TCP and TLS handshake amortized over keep-alive. Throughput targets (Topic 9) are bounded by HTTP parsing speed — modern servers like Envoy and Nginx parse HTTP at millions of requests per second per core. Understanding HTTP's evolution (1.0 → 1.1 → 2 → 3) is essential because each generation changes the latency, throughput, and connection-management math.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server

    Note over C,S: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive (sequential)
    C->>S: GET /users/1  (req #1)
    S->>C: 200 OK  {json}
    C->>S: GET /users/2  (req #2)
    S->>C: 200 OK  {json}

    Note over C,S: HTTP/2 multiplexing (parallel streams on one TCP conn)
    C->>S: GET /users/1  stream=1
    C->>S: GET /users/2  stream=3
    C->>S: GET /users/3  stream=5
    S->>C: 200 OK stream=3 (out of order ok)
    S->>C: 200 OK stream=1
    S->>C: 200 OK stream=5

    Note over C,S: HTTP/3 over QUIC (1-RTT setup incl TLS)
    C->>S: QUIC handshake + HTTP GET (1 flight)
    S->>C: 200 OK
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
HTTP request structure (HTTP/1.1, text):
+----------------------------------------------+
| GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1         <- request line
| Host: api.example.com          <- headers
| Accept: application/json
| Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
| User-Agent: curl/8.0
|                                            <- empty line (CRLF)
| (no body for GET)                          <- optional body
+----------------------------------------------+

HTTP response structure:
+----------------------------------------------+
| HTTP/1.1 200 OK                <- status line
| Content-Type: application/json <- headers
| Content-Length: 38
| Cache-Control: max-age=60
|                                            <- empty line (CRLF)
| {"id":42,"name":"Ada"}                    <- body
+----------------------------------------------+

Status code families:
2xx Success    200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx Redirect   301 Moved, 304 Not Modified
4xx Client err 400 Bad, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many
5xx Server err 500 Internal, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Timeout

HTTP versions (handshake cost per cold request):
HTTP/1.0:  TCP(1.5 RTT)             + req(1 RTT) = 2.5 RTT
HTTP/1.1:  TCP(1.5 RTT)             + req(1 RTT) = 2.5 RTT (keep-alive reuses)
HTTPS 1.1: TCP(1.5 RTT) + TLS1.2(2) + req(1 RTT) = 4.5 RTT
HTTP/2:    TCP(1.5 RTT) + TLS1.2(2) + req(1 RTT) = 4.5 RTT (multiplexed)
HTTP/3:    QUIC(1 RTT, incl TLS1.3) + req(1 RTT) = 2 RTT  (or 1 RTT with 0-RTT)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client opens a TCP connection (or reuses one via keep-alive), sends the request line and headers followed by a blank CRLF line, then optionally the body. The server parses the request, dispatches based on method+path, and produces a status line, headers, blank line, and body.
2. Status code conveys outcome semantics: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client made a mistake (fix the request), 5xx the server failed (retry might help). Headers carry metadata: content type, length, caching directives, authentication.
3. HTTP/2 frames the same logical request into binary frames with a stream ID, allowing many in-flight requests on one TCP connection. HTTP/3 carries the same framing over QUIC streams on UDP, removing the TCP head-of-line blocking that HTTP/2 still has.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Toy HTTP server demonstrating status codes, headers, methods, and idempotency.
- 200 OK -- liveness probe, minimal body
- 400 Bad Request -- client sent garbage
- 200 OK with JSON body
- 404 Not Found -- resource does not exist
- 404 for unknown paths
- Idempotency: a retried POST with the same key returns the cached result.
- 400 Bad Request -- malformed JSON

```python
"""
Toy HTTP server demonstrating status codes, headers, methods, and idempotency.

Run:  python3 http_demo.py
Then: curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/users/42
      curl -i -X POST -d '{"name":"Ada"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
           -H 'Idempotency-Key: abc123' http://127.0.0.1:8080/users
      curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
"""

import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from collections import defaultdict

DB = {1: {"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}}
IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE = {}          # key -> (status, body, headers)
REQUEST_COUNTS = defaultdict(int)

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"   # enables keep-alive

    def _send(self, status: int, body: bytes, headers: dict, content_type="application/json"):
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", content_type)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        for k, v in headers.items():
            self.send_header(k, v)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def do_GET(self):
        REQUEST_COUNTS[self.path] += 1
        if self.path == "/healthz":
            # 200 OK -- liveness probe, minimal body
            self._send(200, b'{"status":"ok"}',
                       {"Cache-Control": "no-store"})
            return
        if self.path.startswith("/users/"):
            try:
                uid = int(self.path.split("/")[-1])
            except ValueError:
                # 400 Bad Request -- client sent garbage
                self._send(400, b'{"error":"invalid id"}', {})
                return
            if uid in DB:
                # 200 OK with JSON body
                self._send(200, json.dumps(DB[uid]).encode(), {})
            else:
                # 404 Not Found -- resource does not exist
                self._send(404, b'{"error":"not found"}', {})
            return
        # 404 for unknown paths
        self._send(404, b'{"error":"unknown route"}', {})

    def do_POST(self):
        if self.path != "/users":
            self._send(404, b'{"error":"unknown route"}', {})
            return

        # Idempotency: a retried POST with the same key returns the cached result.
        idem_key = self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key")
        if idem_key and idem_key in IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE:
            status, body, headers = IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE[idem_key]
            self._send(status, body, headers)
            return

        length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
        try:
            payload = json.loads(self.rfile.read(length) or b"{}")
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            # 400 Bad Request -- malformed JSON
            self._send(400, b'{"error":"invalid json"}', {})
            return

        if "name" not in payload:
            # 422 Unprocessable Entity -- valid JSON, missing required field
            self._send(422, b'{"error":"name required"}', {})
            return

        new_id = max(DB) + 1 if DB else 1
        record = {"id": new_id, "name": payload["name"]}
        DB[new_id] = record
        body = json.dumps(record).encode()
        headers = {"Location": f"/users/{new_id}"}
        if idem_key:
            IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE[idem_key] = (201, body, headers)
        # 201 Created with Location header pointing at the new resource
        self._send(201, body, headers)

    def do_DELETE(self):
        if not self.path.startswith("/users/"):
            self._send(404, b'{"error":"unknown route"}', {})
            return
        try:
            uid = int(self.path.split("/")[-1])
        except ValueError:
            self._send(400, b'{"error":"invalid id"}', {})
            return
        if uid in DB:
            del DB[uid]
            # 204 No Content -- successful, no body to return
            self._send(204, b"", {})
        else:
            # DELETE is idempotent: deleting a missing resource is still 204
            self._send(204, b"", {})

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        # Show method + path + status so you can see status codes change.
        print(f"  {self.command} {self.path} -> {args[1]}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8080), Handler)
    print("listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080  (try: /users/1, /healthz, /users/99)")
    try:
        srv.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nrequests seen:", dict(REQUEST_COUNTS))
        srv.shutdown()
```

quiz.question: What does it mean that HTTP is "stateless," and how do real applications build sessions on top of it?
options: A method is "safe" if it has no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) — calling it must not change server state.
401 means "I don't know who you are" — the client failed to authenticate.
Content negotiation is the mechanism by which client and server agree on the representation of a resource.
HTTP is stateless at the protocol level: each request carries all the context the server needs to handle it, and the server is not required to remember anything about previous requests.
quiz.explanation: HTTP is stateless at the protocol level: each request carries all the context the server needs to handle it, and the server is not required to remember anything about previous requests. This is what makes HTTP horizontally scalable — any instance can handle any request because there's no per-connection server-side state in the spec.

quiz.question: What is the difference between HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing?
options: 401 means "I don't know who you are" — the client failed to authenticate.

quiz.explanation: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive lets a single TCP connection carry multiple requests, but they must be sequential — the client sends request 1, waits for the response, then sends request 2. This avoids the TCP/TLS handshake cost per request but still suffers head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer: a slow request blocks all later requests on the same connection.

quiz.explanation: A method is "safe" if it has no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) — calling it must not change server state. A method is "idempotent" if calling it N times has the same effect as calling it once (GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD). POST is neither safe nor idempotent — each POST may create a new resource, so a retried POST after a network timeout could create duplicate orders.

quiz.explanation: 200 OK is the default success. 201 Created is success with a new resource (POST that creates), typically with a Location header. 204 No Content is success with no body (DELETE, PUT with no echo).

quiz.explanation: Content negotiation is the mechanism by which client and server agree on the representation of a resource. The client sends Accept: application/json (or application/protobuf, text/html, image/webp) and Accept-Language: en-US, and the server picks a representation it can produce, returning it with Content-Type: application/json.
